removed_share.hiring.label: Hiring posts later removed
removed_share.hiring.description: Share of hiring posts from the first 7 days that were deleted or killed before we fetched the thread. It depends on how long after the window we fetched (years for old months, about a day for new ones), so it is for the methodology note only and not comparable across months.

removed_share.seeking.label: Job seeker posts later removed
removed_share.seeking.description: Share of “Who wants to be hired?” posts from the first 7 days that were deleted or killed before we fetched the thread. It depends on how long after the window we fetched, so it is for the methodology note only and not comparable across months.

posts.hiring.label: Hiring posts
posts.hiring.description: Top-level posts in the first 7 days of the monthly Hacker News “Who is hiring?” thread, including ones later deleted. One post often covers several roles, so this counts posts, not jobs.

posts.seeking.label: People looking for work
posts.seeking.description: Top-level posts in the first 7 days of the monthly “Who wants to be hired?” thread, including ones later deleted.

seekers_per_post.hiring.label: Job seekers per hiring post
seekers_per_post.hiring.description: Posts from people who want work divided by posts from companies hiring, in the same month. Both counts include posts later deleted.

seekers_per_post_us.hiring.label: US job seekers per hiring post open to US workers
seekers_per_post_us.hiring.description: Job seekers per hiring post, counting only seekers whose Location line is in the US and hiring posts whose first line names a US place or offers remote work US workers can take (no region stated, or the US, North America, the Americas, worldwide or US time zones). Both counts include posts later deleted. Deleted posts, seekers whose location we can't place, and hiring posts that name no place and don't mention remote work are assumed to split the same way as the rest. Shown only when at least 50 seekers have a known location.

replies_per_post.hiring.label: Replies per job post
replies_per_post.hiring.description: Average number of direct replies a job post got in its first 7 days.

salary_disclosed_share.hiring.label: Posts that show pay
salary_disclosed_share.hiring.description: Share of job posts that state a yearly salary figure or range, in any currency. Hourly rates, equity and funding amounts don’t count. Posts from 2011–12 are about half as long as later ones, so early shares run low.

salary_min_median_usd.hiring.label: Typical bottom of the pay range
salary_min_median_usd.hiring.description: Median across posts of each post’s typical low end of pay (the median of its ranges’ lows), among posts that give yearly pay in US dollars.

salary_max_median_usd.hiring.label: Typical top of the pay range
salary_max_median_usd.hiring.description: Median across posts of each post’s typical high end of pay (the median of its ranges’ highs), among posts that give yearly pay in US dollars.

remote_token_share.hiring.label: Posts that say remote
remote_token_share.hiring.description: Share of job posts whose first line mentions remote work (and doesn’t rule it out). Starts in July 2015, when the REMOTE/ONSITE header convention took hold.

onsite_token_share.hiring.label: Posts that say onsite
onsite_token_share.hiring.description: Share of job posts whose first line says the job is onsite. Starts in July 2015, when the REMOTE/ONSITE header convention took hold.

visa_share.hiring.label: Posts that offer visa help
visa_share.hiring.description: Share of job posts that offer visa sponsorship or transfers. Posts that say they can’t sponsor are not counted. Posts from 2011–12 are about half as long as later ones, so early shares run low.

new_company_share.hiring.label: New or returning after two years
new_company_share.hiring.description: Share of companies posting that had not posted in any of the previous 24 months’ threads. Starts in April 2013, the first month with a full 24 months of history behind it.

returning_company_share.hiring.label: Back from last month
returning_company_share.hiring.description: Share of companies posting that also posted the month before.

ai_native_share.hiring.label: Posts describing an AI product
ai_native_share.hiring.description: Expected share of job posts from companies whose product is built on AI or machine learning, as judged by a language model reading each post.

new_grad_share.hiring.label: Open to new grads
new_grad_share.hiring.description: Expected share of job posts open to new graduates or junior engineers, as judged by a language model reading each post.

seeker_mood.seeking.label: Job seeker mood
seeker_mood.seeking.description: Average mood of “Who wants to be hired?” posts on a 0 (discouraged) to 4 (upbeat) scale, as judged by a language model reading each post.

seeker_strained_share.seeking.label: Job seekers under strain
seeker_strained_share.seeking.description: Expected share of “Who wants to be hired?” posts that sound discouraged or strained: a long search, a layoff, urgency or money worries, as judged by a language model.

seeker_us_share.seeking.label: Job seekers in the US
seeker_us_share.seeking.description: Share of “Who wants to be hired?” posts whose Location line is in the US, among posts whose Location line names a place we recognize.

eng_leadership_share.hiring.label: Hiring engineering leads
eng_leadership_share.hiring.description: Expected share of job posts hiring engineering managers or leads, as judged by a language model reading each post.

interns_token_share.hiring.label: Posts that mention interns
interns_token_share.hiring.description: Share of job posts that mention interns or internships anywhere in the text. Posts from 2011–12 are about half as long as later ones, so early shares run low.

years_required_median.hiring.label: Typical years of experience asked for
years_required_median.hiring.description: Median across posts of the fewest years of experience each post asks for (“3-5 years” counts as 3; a post with several roles counts its lowest), among posts that state a number. Company age, runway and the team’s own years are not counted.

years_required_share.hiring.label: Posts that state years of experience
years_required_share.hiring.description: Share of job posts that ask for a stated number of years of experience. Posts from 2011–12 are about half as long as later ones, so early shares run low.

degree_required_share.hiring.label: Posts that ask for a degree
degree_required_share.hiring.description: Share of job posts that require or prefer a degree (BS, MS, PhD, a CS degree) and don’t say experience can stand in for it. Posts from 2011–12 are about half as long as later ones, so early shares run low.

degree_optional_share.hiring.label: Posts that say a degree is optional
degree_optional_share.hiring.description: Share of job posts that say a degree isn’t needed or that equivalent experience will do (“or equivalent experience”, “no degree required”). Posts from 2011–12 are about half as long as later ones, so early shares run low.

post_length_median.hiring.label: Typical post length
post_length_median.hiring.description: Median length of a job post in characters, after HTML is stripped.

interview_style_share.hiring.label: Posts that describe the interview
interview_style_share.hiring.description: Share of job posts that say how they interview: a take-home, no LeetCode or whiteboard, a pair-programming session, or a paid trial. Posts from 2011–12 are about half as long as later ones, so early shares run low.

office_days_share.hiring.label: Posts that state office days
office_days_share.hiring.description: Share of job posts that say how many days a week to be in the office (“3 days a week in office”, “hybrid, 2 days”, “onsite Mon–Fri”). Posts from 2011–12 are about half as long as later ones, so early shares run low.

stack.description: Each category is its own share of hiring posts, so they do not add up to 100%. A mention is not usage: a post can name a tool it is replacing or one it would like to try.

stack_ai_ml.description: Each category is its own share of hiring posts, so they do not add up to 100%. A mention is not usage: a post can name a tool it is replacing or one it would like to try.

stack_mobile.label: Mobile platforms job posts mention
stack_mobile.description: Each category is its own share of hiring posts, so they do not add up to 100%. A mention is not usage: a post can name a tool it is replacing or one it would like to try.

benefits.label: Benefits job posts offer
benefits.description: Share of hiring posts that offer each benefit; posts that rule one out (“no equity”, “we can’t sponsor visas”) don’t count. Vague phrases (“great benefits”, “generous PTO”) don’t count either. Paid time off, days stated means a number of days or weeks. Visa uses the same rule as visa_share. Each category is its own share. Equity's rise since 2021 is mostly disclosure: among posts that state pay, equity mentions held at 40–59%; most of the rise comes from more posts stating pay (“$X + equity”).

years_required.label: Years of experience asked for
years_required.description: Among posts that state years of experience, the share whose smallest stated number falls in each band.

interview_style.label: How job posts say they interview
interview_style.description: Share of hiring posts that mention each interview style. “No LeetCode” counts posts that say they skip LeetCode, whiteboard or puzzle questions. Each category is its own share.

region.label: Where hiring posts are, by region
region.description: A header can name several regions, so shares do not add up to 100%.

seeker_region.label: Where job seekers are, by region

sec_restructuring_usd.US.label: Restructuring and other charges, US public tech panel
sec_restructuring_usd.US.credit: SEC EDGAR filings; panel and sums by this report
sec_restructuring_usd.US.description: Restructuring and other charges for one calendar quarter, summed over the SEC panel (the 50 largest US software, internet and chip companies by revenue, fixed each January; chips include Amkor, which packages and tests them, and leave out solar makers). Each company-year uses the first of these XBRL tags it reported: RestructuringCharges, SeveranceCosts1, RestructuringAndRelatedCostIncurredCost, RestructuringSettlementAndImpairmentProvisions, RestructuringCosts, RestructuringCostsAndAssetImpairmentCharges; some include impairments and other exit costs, and a few carry other items (Intel's 2021-Q1 value includes the VLSI patent litigation charge). Meta files its charges under its own XBRL element and is left out. A charge reported only in the 10-K, with no quarter, counts in sec_restructuring_companies but adds no dollars here (annual_only lists those companies; Salesforce's $828 million for fiscal 2023 is one), so the sum understates. n is the number of companies with dollars; top names the largest and its share of the total. The quarter is the latest that every company had to file by the as-of date, so it trails the HN month by four to six months. The same quarter is shown for three HN months, and its value can change between them as late filers arrive. Each month shows the value as first published by that month's as-of date; later revisions are not applied.

sec_restructuring_companies.US.label: Panel companies reporting restructuring charges
sec_restructuring_companies.US.credit: SEC EDGAR filings; panel and counts by this report
sec_restructuring_companies.US.description: Number of companies in the SEC panel (the 50 largest US software, internet and chip companies by revenue, fixed each January; chips include Amkor, which packages and tests them, and leave out solar makers) that reported a restructuring or similar charge for the quarter (tags as in sec_restructuring_usd; Meta, which uses its own element, is left out). A charge reported only for the full year counts in the fiscal year's last quarter. Sturdier than the dollar sum, which one large charge can dominate. n is the number of companies counted. The same quarter is shown for three HN months, and its value can change between them as late filers arrive. Each month shows the value as first published by that month's as-of date; later revisions are not applied.

sec_item_205_filings_panel.US.label: Layoff filings (8-K Item 2.05), US public tech panel
sec_item_205_filings_panel.US.credit: SEC EDGAR filings; panel and counts by this report
sec_item_205_filings_panel.US.description: 8-K filings (not amendments) that report Item 2.05, exit or disposal costs, with an EDGAR filing date in the calendar month before the HN month, by the SEC panel (the 50 largest US software, internet and chip companies by revenue, fixed each January; chips include Amkor, which packages and tests them, and leave out solar makers); n is the panel size. Item 2.05 is required only for a committed plan with material costs, so it rarely captures big tech layoffs: Meta's 11,000 job cuts in November 2022 came with no Item 2.05 filing. Each month shows the value as first published by that month's as-of date; later revisions are not applied.

sec_item_205_filings_software.US.label: Layoff filings (8-K Item 2.05), all software and IT-services filers
sec_item_205_filings_software.US.credit: SEC EDGAR filings; counts by this report
sec_item_205_filings_software.US.description: 8-K filings (not amendments) that report Item 2.05, exit or disposal costs, with an EDGAR filing date in the calendar month before the HN month, by any company whose filing header carried SIC code 7370-7374 (computer programming, software, systems design, data processing) when it filed. Item 2.05 rarely captures big tech layoffs (Meta filed none for its November 2022 cuts). Each month shows the value as first published by that month's as-of date; later revisions are not applied.

sec_headcount_panel.US.label: Employees at US public tech panel companies, change over a year
sec_headcount_panel.US.credit: SEC EDGAR filings; counts read from 10-K text and summed by this report
sec_headcount_panel.US.description: Year-over-year change in employees across the SEC panel (the 50 largest US software, internet and chip companies by revenue, fixed each January; chips include Amkor, which packages and tests them, and leave out solar makers), from the employee count in each company's latest 10-K against its previous 10-K, over the companies that state both; n is that number of companies. 10-Ks come once a year, so the series moves as each company files. Amazon has about a third of the panel's employees, mostly warehouse and delivery staff, so it drives this total; sec_headcount_median_yoy shows the typical company. Each point lists the companies behind it (companies, as CIKs); the set changes from month to month as 10-Ks arrive. A company that completed any deal between its two 10-Ks or within 75 days after the later one (an 8-K with Items 2.01 and 9.01, its own Form 10, or a hand-checked split such as HP's or eBay's PayPal spin-off) is left out when its count also changed by more than 15%. That rule also drops some years whose growth was mostly organic (Uber 2020, ServiceNow 2021, Meta 2014). A change of more than about 100% up or 50% down with no deal is treated as a misread count and left out too. Left-out companies are listed with the reason (dropped). Each month shows the value as first published by that month's as-of date; later revisions are not applied.

sec_headcount_median_yoy.US.label: Employees at the median US public tech panel company, change over a year
sec_headcount_median_yoy.US.credit: SEC EDGAR filings; counts read from 10-K text; median by this report
sec_headcount_median_yoy.US.description: Median company's year-over-year change in employees across the SEC panel (the 50 largest US software, internet and chip companies by revenue, fixed each January; chips include Amkor, which packages and tests them, and leave out solar makers), from each company's latest 10-K against its previous 10-K, over the companies that state both (the same companies as sec_headcount_panel); n is that number. Unlike the total, no single company drives it. Many companies round their count ("approximately 19,000") and some repeat it from year to year, so the median can sit at exactly zero for months at a time. Each point lists the companies behind it (companies, as CIKs); the set changes from month to month as 10-Ks arrive. A company that completed any deal between its two 10-Ks or within 75 days after the later one (an 8-K with Items 2.01 and 9.01, its own Form 10, or a hand-checked split such as HP's or eBay's PayPal spin-off) is left out when its count also changed by more than 15%. That rule also drops some years whose growth was mostly organic (Uber 2020, ServiceNow 2021, Meta 2014). A change of more than about 100% up or 50% down with no deal is treated as a misread count and left out too. Left-out companies are listed with the reason (dropped). Each month shows the value as first published by that month's as-of date; later revisions are not applied.

sources.name: Hacker News hiring threads
sources.measures: Employer posts in the monthly “Ask HN: Who is hiring?” thread and posts from people looking for work in “Who wants to be hired?”, read in the first 7 days. The job-seeker thread began in May 2014.
sources.lag: None: each issue reads that month's threads once their first week is over.
sources.caveat: A startup-leaning panel, not the market: it skews toward venture-backed companies, engineering roles and the Bay Area, many posters are outside the US, and one post can list many roles.

sources.name: Indeed Hiring Lab
sources.measures: Software development job postings on Indeed in the US and UK (an index, February 2020 = 100), the share offering remote or hybrid work, and the share that state pay.
sources.lag: Days for postings; the remote share runs to the previous month end and pay transparency about two months behind.
sources.caveat: Postings are ads, not hires, and Indeed's mix of sites and employers changes over time. The remote and pay shares are not seasonally adjusted.

sources.name: BLS Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS)
sources.measures: Job openings, hires and layoffs in the information sector and in professional and business services, all occupations, US.
sources.lag: About two months: an issue carries the newest month published by its date.
sources.caveat: Industries, not occupations: these counts include every job in those sectors, not only software work. Not seasonally adjusted, so compare a month with the same month a year earlier, or use the 12-month average.
sources.credit: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, JOLTS; vintages via ALFRED

sources.name: BLS Current Employment Statistics (CES)
sources.measures: People employed by computer systems design and related services firms (NAICS 5415), US, seasonally adjusted.
sources.caveat: An industry, not an occupation, and it leaves out software engineers employed elsewhere. Values are as first published, so BLS's annual benchmark revision shows up as a step in early-year months.
sources.credit: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics; vintages via ALFRED

sources.name: SEC EDGAR filings
sources.measures: Headcount, restructuring costs and layoff filings from a fixed panel of US tech companies.
sources.lag: Quarterly or annual, dated by each filing's acceptance time.
sources.caveat: Large public companies only, and headcount is company-wide, not engineering.
